common_name: Moroccan Mint (Classic Culinary Spearmint for Tea)

planting.note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; plant in partial shade in consistently moist, fertile soil and contain the roots to stop rampant spread.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Moroccan Mint is the classic spearmint selection traditionally used for Moroccan mint tea, prized for its clean, sweet, true spearmint flavor without the sharper menthol bite of peppermint, making it the standard choice for hot mint tea sweetened with sugar as well as for cocktails like mojitos and juleps. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather to prevent wilting, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut the planting back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage for the rest of the growing season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Herb Gardening

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Golden Sage is a variegated culinary sage cultivar with leaves edged and mottled in golden-yellow, distinct from the older Icterina, Berggarten, Tricolor, and Purple sage selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; sage rots readily in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil, so good drainage is essential, especially through humid Gulf South summers. Golden Sage bears the same savory, aromatic culinary flavor as common garden sage in leaves brightly variegated with golden-yellow margins, providing ornamental color to an herb garden or border in addition to a full culinary harvest. It flowers in early summer with small blue-violet blooms attractive to bees, and the plant develops a woody, shrubby base over time like other garden sages. Harvest leaves as needed through the growing season, and prune lightly after flowering and again in early spring to keep the plant compact and prevent it from becoming leggy and woody in the center.
